item.title: We want to make Dhaka as clean as Tokyo: PM
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Wednesday said his government was working to make Dhaka and the rest of the country clean, pollution-free and healthy, aiming to transform the capital into a city as clean as Tokyo.

“We are trying to make Dhaka and the entire country clean. Initiatives are being taken to reduce air pollution, improve the environment and plant trees in different places,” he said.

The Prime Minister made the remarks while responding to questions from expatriate Bangladeshis at an exchange of views, organised by the Bangladesh Community, an organisation of Bangladeshis living in Japan, at Hotel New Otani in Tokyo this evening.

Referring to the cleanliness of Tokyo's streets, Tarique Rahman said garbage was rarely seen on the city's roads, in contrast to Dhaka, where waste accumulated in different places.

He said the situation needed to change as waste could spread germs and make people sick. Maintaining a clean environment and ensuring proper waste disposal were essential to protecting public health, he said.

“If we can make Dhaka as clean as Tokyo, as Japan, that will be a major reform for the people,” he said.

The Prime Minister said the government's reform priorities were focused on improving the lives of marginalised and working-class people, ensuring that the benefits of initiatives in education, healthcare and the environment reached people from all walks of life.

He said rickshaw pullers, CNG-run auto-rickshaw drivers, doctors, lawyers, teachers, service holders and businesspeople would all benefit from such initiatives.

“As a politician, I understand reform to mean the kind of reform whose benefits reach the marginalised people. There are different kinds of reforms. There are reforms in air-conditioned rooms, and there are also reforms aimed at making the lives of working people a little better,” he said.

Tarique Rahman said the government prioritised initiatives that would improve ordinary people's living standards, adding that he attached greater importance to measures benefiting working people because he sought their votes.

He called for the cooperation of all democratic-minded people to implement the reforms and build the Bangladesh they aspired to.

The Prime Minister said attempts were being made to create obstacles to prevent the BNP government from implementing reforms that would benefit ordinary people.

Addressing expatriate Bangladeshis, he said the reform initiatives undertaken by the government would benefit people across the country, including the families of expatriates, and urged them to support the initiatives.

“I am not asking you to vote for us. If you think these initiatives are right, then support the work so that we can implement them,” he said.

Referring to satire and ridicule on social media concerning Aam Janata Party Member Secretary Md Tarek Rahman, the Prime Minister said that although he was the subject of considerable criticism, there was little discussion of the country's various problems.

He reiterated that the government's goal was to implement reforms in education, healthcare, the environment and other areas to improve people's living standards. 

While some reforms might benefit a limited number of people, he said, his priority was to pursue initiatives that would benefit a broader section of the society.

He stressed that hard work, patience and unity were needed to accomplish the tasks and sought the cooperation and prayers of expatriate Bangladeshis for the country's development.

At the beginning of the programme, the Prime Minister answered questions from expatriate Bangladeshis on various issues, including plans to help children develop proficiency in Japanese and build skills in healthcare, sports and other fields, simplify business procedures, reopen closed industrial units, increase investment and create employment.

Prime Minister's wife Dr Zubaida Rahman also attended the event, moderated by BNP Executive Committee member Abdus Sattar Patwary.

Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury, Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M. Rashiduzzaman Millat, Prime Minister's Adviser on Finance and Planning Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Aninda Islam Amit, Invest Bangladesh Authority Chairman Ashik Chowdhury and other members of the Prime Minister's entourage attended the event.

The Japan unit of BNP presented photographs to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and his wife, Dr Zubaida Rahman, at the event.

item.title: Plan International Bangladesh launches ResCoast project to strengthen climate resilience
item.description:
Plan International Bangladesh, in partnership with Standard Chartered Bank Bangladesh, organised an inception workshop for the Building Climate Resilient, Environment Sustainable Coastal Communities (ResCoast) project in Barguna sadar upazila, reports a press release.

The workshop brought together government officials, local government representatives, development partners and community stakeholders to introduce the project's objectives, strengthen coordination and identify opportunities for collaboration towards building climate-resilient coastal communities.

Funded by Standard Chartered Bank under its Agriculture Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiative, the ResCoast project aims to strengthen climate resilience, promote green livelihoods and advance environmental sustainability in vulnerable coastal communities.

Implemented in Barguna, the project will directly support 1,815 vulnerable coastal households across six climate-resilient villages, with a particular focus on young women and youths aged 18–24.

The workshop was attended by Md Shah Aziz, upazila nirbahi officer (UNO), Barguna Sadar, as chief guest, and chaired by Md Anamul Hoque, director, Resource Development Foundation (RDF). Special guests included Md Sakhawat Hossain, upazila Agriculture Officer; Bithi Debnath, upazila livestock officer; Maruf Hossain Minar, senior upazila fisheries officer; Md Ziad Hasan, upazila secondary education officer; and Md Muzammel Hossain Bhuiyan, assistant conservator of Forests. Chairpersons from unions, NGO representatives, journalists, farmers' representatives and other project stakeholders also participated.

Speaking as Chief Guest, Md Shah Aziz, upazila nirbahi officer, Barguna Sadar, highlighted, “Building climate-resilient communities requires more than individual efforts; it demands strong collaboration between government institutions, development partners and local communities. The ResCoast project presents an important opportunity to work together towards sustainable livelihoods, environmental protection and long-term resilience in Barguna.”

The workshop featured a detailed presentation outlining the project's objectives, planned interventions and implementation approach. It highlighted key focus areas, including climate-smart agriculture, sustainable fisheries and livestock management, strengthening community-based climate resilience, promoting youth leadership, and advancing gender equality and social inclusion.

The special guests welcomed the initiative, expressed their commitment to supporting its implementation and emphasised the importance of inclusive participation and coordination among relevant government departments and community stakeholders. The workshop also provided an opportunity to establish a shared understanding of the project's priorities, identify areas for institutional collaboration, discuss potential risks and mitigation measures, and review key implementation milestones. Moving forward, the project will work closely with relevant government departments and local stakeholders to promote coordinated interventions, strengthen community ownership and support the long-term sustainability of its outcomes.

Through ResCoast project, Plan International Bangladesh aims to support climate-vulnerable coastal communities in adopting sustainable livelihood practices, strengthening their capacity to adapt to climate change and promoting the meaningful participation and leadership of youths and women in building a more resilient future.

item.title: Spain train collision kills at least 31, injures 80
item.description:
SPAIN-ACCIDENT-TRANSPORT-TRAIN

A high-speed train collision south of Madrid killed 31 people and injured 80 on Wednesday, with the toll likely to rise, regional authorities said, in Spain's second such disaster this year.

AFP reporters on the scene in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha saw one train embedded into another and some carriages lying on their side in tangles of metal debris at the bottom of an embankment.

Dozens of emergency services vehicles were racing to and from the site and helicopters hovered above during a frantic search for survivors.

A spokeswoman from the Castilla-La Mancha government told AFP at least 31 people had died and that another 80 were injured.

Castilla-La Mancha's leader Emiliano Garcia-Page told reporters that more victims were likely as "it has not yet been possible to reach the bottom of the carriages."

State railway operator Renfe confirmed in a statement that the main high-speed line from Madrid to southern Spain had been suspended after one of its services suffered an accident with a train from private Spanish company Iryo.

A spokesperson for the Spanish emergency services told AFP the trains collided just before 9:00 am (0800 GMT) in the municipality of Urda, around 130 kilometres (80 miles) south of Madrid.

Rail safety under scrutiny

The accident comes one month before Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who faced heavy criticism for this year's first disaster, seeks to overturn unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership in an early general election on 29 November.

Sanchez said on X that he was "shocked" by the accident and sent "my love, solidarity and support to all the victims and their families".

He cancelled his participation in a summit on obesity in Madrid after the news broke, while his Socialist party suspended all its campaign activities.

Condolences flooded in from across Spain and Europe. The Spanish royal household said on X it was "shocked and concerned" by the accident, conveying its support to the victims, their loved ones and the emergency services.

An EU spokeswoman said the bloc was "ready to help Spain if needed", while European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen said "Europe mourns" with the victims after the "devastating news".

Spain's high-speed rail network has received huge investment in recent years, growing to become the world's second-largest after China and a source of national pride.

But Wednesday's accident comes after another collision between two high-speed trains outside the southern village of Adamuz in January left 46 dead, which raised major questions about safety on the country's railways.

That crash was Spain's deadliest train accident since 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the northwestern city of Santiago de Compostela.

Both of this year's accidents happened on the line linking Madrid to the southern city of Seville.

One of the country's busiest routes, it was Spain's first high-speed line when it opened in 1992 to coincide with the Seville universal exposition.

item.title: SAU students vandalise fair structures over Secretariat relocation plan
item.description:
Students of Sher-e-Bangla Agricultural University (SAU) have been protesting for several days against a move to relocate the Secretariat to the old trade fair ground in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, the capital.

As part of their protest, students vandalised structures under construction for two fairs at the venue on Wednesday morning. University authorities later intervened and brought the students back to campus.

Police and people involved in organising the fairs said two events were being organised side by side at the old trade fair ground. Preparations were underway for a month-long event titled the Asia International Trade Fair. Another fair, called the Youth Fair, was also being organised nearby for a week. Gates and various stalls were being constructed at the venue for the two events.

People involved in the fair arrangements alleged that 70 to 80 SAU students went to the site on Wednesday morning and vandalised the structures. They carried out the destruction under a banner reading, “We want our research field back, not the Secretariat.”

A police team was present at the scene but failed to stop the students, they said. The organisers alleged that the incident caused financial losses and that construction materials were also taken away.

A visit to the site around noon found that part of the corrugated metal fencing erected for the fairs had been demolished. Several wooden structures intended for stalls lay on the ground, while workers involved in building the stalls were dismantling them.

Yusuf Sardar, who was involved in constructing stalls for the Youth Fair, told Prothom Alo that they were building the stalls with government permission. If anyone had objections to using the fairground, they should take the matter up with the government, he said.

“Why were the stalls vandalised? What have we done wrong?” he asked.

He also alleged that the students had taken away tools and equipment used to construct the stalls after carrying out the vandalism.

A person involved in setting up stalls for the Asia International Trade Fair, who requested anonymity, said the main entrance to their fair had been vandalised. More than 100 students had arrived, damaged the structures and then left, he alleged. The incident had caused losses amounting to several lakh taka, he added.

Asked about the vandalism, SAU acting proctor Professor Tajul Islam told Prothom Alo that students had been protesting for several days against the plan to relocate the Secretariat to the old trade fair ground.

“The administration will take initiatives to address their demands. We will take steps to ensure that incidents such as vandalism do not happen again,” he said.

The students maintain that the old trade fair ground belongs to their university and that they will not allow the Secretariat to be built there. They are demanding that the ground be returned to the university for research purposes.

On Tuesday, soil testing was underway at the fairground as part of preparations for the proposed Secretariat relocation. At noon, university students marched to the site and took soil-testing equipment and two vehicles to their campus.

They also boycotted classes and examinations that day. The students have formed a steering committee to press their demand for the return of the ground.

item.title: Why people detained for criticising govt
item.description:
What is the crime of Sathi Akter, a female entrepreneur from Bhaluka? She expressed her frustration over repeated thefts at her business establishment. In a Facebook live, she said, “Suffering due to voting for the BNP government.”

Angered by Sathi Akter’s statement, local BNP leaders and activists surrounded her business establishment, demanding justice. Subsequently, the police took her into custody and later arrested and sent her to court, which then sent her to jail.

As a citizen, she shared her experience, sought security from the government, and expressed disappointment over her voting decision. What could be more ordinary in a democratic state? Yet the situation she faced is not just a case of harassment of a female entrepreneur; it raises serious questions about the ruling party, police, and judiciary’s stance towards freedom of expression and dissent.

Sathi Akter has been in business for about 14 years. According to her, electrical wires were stolen from her shop multiple times recently, and similar thefts occurred in neighbouring shops. These incidents have caused her financial losses. It is the responsibility of law enforcement to prevent theft and ensure the security of businesses. Thus, she has ample reason to express her frustration.

However, instead of addressing this issue, local BNP leaders and activists gathered in front of her business establishment, almost like a mob. A local Swechchhasebok Dal leader told Prothom Alo that party activists were angry over the alleged derogatory remarks about BNP and wanted to resist the woman. The question is, where did they get the right to ‘resist’ a citizen just because they didn’t like what she said?

The police’s role is even more surprising. The officer-in-charge of Bhaluka police station stated that he viewed the video multiple times and found Sathi’s statement to fall under freedom of speech. According to him, tension arose because the woman acted aggressively with some businessmen, leading to her arrest under section 151 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

A statement may seem offensive or objectionable. It can be protested. But it is extremely concerning to detain someone due to dissatisfaction, and for the police to arrest them under the Anti-Terrorism Act. To consider a statement as an act of terrorism, specific elements and evidence related to the relevant law are required. Making offensive remarks about a leader of the ruling party cannot be an alternative to that evidence.

The police’s explanation is misleading. What role did those who surrounded her business establishment play in inciting tension? Why was the person making the statement arrested under the pretext of controlling the situation? Section 151 of the Code of Criminal Procedure can be applied to prevent a potential cognizable offence. Merely causing tension does not justify arresting someone under this section.

If someone feels aggrieved by a statement, they can follow a legal path. However, encircling a business, creating a frightening situation, and handing the person making the statement over to the police, demanding justice, is not the rule of law. Such incidents send a terrible message to others—they may face all sorts of harassment, legal and illegal, for criticising the ruling party.

Not an isolated incident

There is a resemblance between the Bhaluka incident and an event on 2 April in Sreenagar of Munshiganj. Local BNP and Jubo Dal leaders and activists gathered at the restaurant of Shaon Mahmud, accused of making alleged derogatory remarks on Facebook about Prime Minister Tarique Rahman. They detained Shaon and handed him over to the police, who arrested him under the Anti-Terrorism Act.

According to a report by Jamuna Television, the Jubo Dal leaders and activists present at the scene said they could not tolerate the post critical of the Prime Minister. The police also stated that party activists detained Shaon and handed him over. Human Rights Watch highlighted the incident as an example of treating expression as a crime under pressure from government supporters.

Both the government and BNP's top leadership must take a clear stance on this issue. Party activists must stop acting like mobsters by surrounding someone’s house or business due to dissatisfaction with their statements, detaining them, or pressuring the police to take action against them. At the same time, the police must step away from the culture of political allegiance. To protect democracy, human rights, and freedom of expression, this must be done.

A statement may seem offensive or objectionable. It can be protested. But it is extremely concerning to detain someone due to dissatisfaction, and for the police to arrest them under the Anti-Terrorism Act. To consider a statement as an act of terrorism, specific elements and evidence related to the relevant law are required. Making offensive remarks about a leader of the ruling party cannot be an alternative to that evidence.

There are many more examples of similar incidents; businesses have been encircled somewhere, party activists have detained someone and handed them over to the police, and there have been allegations of attacks centering on online reactions. In all these incidents, a trend is evident: a section of the ruling party takes the law into their own hands in response to dissent, criticism, or negative reactions; and by observing police operations, it seems they act more on party directives than securing citizens' rights.

A gap between promises and reality

BNP leaders and activists faced cases, arrests, and harassment while in opposition for a long time. The party should not be unaware of the experience of curtailed freedom of expression. BNP has criticised the Awami League government for the alleged use of various laws, including the Digital Security Act, to harass journalists, opposition activists, and ordinary citizens.

BNP also promised to ensure freedom of expression for citizens regardless of political identity if they came to power. The evaluation of that promise lies in how the government and the party treat those who speak against the government.

Article 39 of the Constitution recognises freedom of thought, conscience, and expression, although it also provides for reasonable restrictions by law. These restrictions cannot be used as a shield against criticism of the ruling party or leaders.

The government, party, and state are not synonymous. Criticising the government is not a crime against the state; rather, demanding accountability for the government’s actions is a democratic right.

Both the government and BNP's top leadership must take a clear stance on this issue. Party activists must stop acting like mobsters by surrounding someone’s house or business due to dissatisfaction with their statements, detaining them, or pressuring the police to take action against them. At the same time, the police must step away from the culture of political allegiance. To protect democracy, human rights, and freedom of expression, this must be done.

item.title: Shadman on 99 as Bangladesh end day one at 213-3 against West Indies
item.description:
Shadman Islam remained unbeaten on 99 as Bangladesh finished the opening day of the first Test against West Indies at 213 for three after bad light interrupted play at the Sher-e-Bangla National Cricket Stadium in Mirpur on Wednesday.

Shadman, who struck his 10th Test half-century earlier in the day, was left stranded one run short of his third Test century when the umpires called off play with Bangladesh having batted for 74 overs.

The left-handed opener faced 219 ball and anchored the innings after Bangladesh lost an early wicket, combining patience with increasingly assured strokeplay to put the hosts in a strong position.

The day's final interruption came after a brief resumption following an earlier stoppage for bad light. With the conditions still unsuitable for fast bowling, the umpires decided to suspend play again, denying Shadman an opportunity to reach his century before stumps.

Bangladesh will resume on the second morning with Shadman on 99 and Litton Das unbeaten on seven.

Shadman anchors Bangladesh's recovery

West Indies made an encouraging start with the new ball, as pacers Jayden Seales and Shamar Joseph maintained tight lines and troubled the Bangladesh openers.

Their efforts paid off in the seventh over when Seales dismissed Tanzid Hasan for seven. Tanzid attempted to play a delivery outside off stump through the cover region, but the ball took the outside edge and flew to Greaves at second slip.

Bangladesh were reduced to 9 for one, and Shadman initially struggled to get off the mark, taking 16 deliveries to score his first run.

However, he gradually settled into his innings and found an effective partner in Mominul Haque. The pair counterattacked sensibly, rotating the strike and taking advantage of scoring opportunities to rebuild the innings.
Their second-wicket partnership was worth 59 runs before Mominul departed for 28.

Trying to loft a delivery from left-arm spinner Jomel Warrican over mid-off, Mominul stepped out of his crease but failed to make proper contact. Shamar Joseph, stationed at mid-off, completed the catch.

Shadman continued to hold the innings together, reaching his 10th Test half-century in 34th  over as Bangladesh moved past 100.

He was joined by captain Najmul Hossain Shanto, but the partnership lasted only until the 36th over. Najmul, on 19, attempted a sweep against Warrican and missed the ball. West Indies captain Roston Chase opted for a review after the on-field umpire turned down the appeal. The replay showed that the ball had pitched in line, struck the batter in line and would have hit the middle and leg stumps.

Bangladesh were 112 for three, leaving Shadman to rebuild once more.

Towhid Hridoy joined Shadman and helped Bangladesh regain control.

The pair batted with contrasting approaches. While Shadman concentrated on building his innings, Hridoy looked to score more freely, helping Bangladesh maintain momentum.

Their partnership carried Bangladesh past 150. By the end of the second session, Shadman was unbeaten on 79, while Hridoy had contributed 39.

However, Hridoy's promising innings ended prematurely after he suffered severe cramp in his left leg.

The Bangladesh batter received treatment on the field after going down near the crease during the 65th over. Although he initially recovered, he was unable to continue after taking a single two deliveries later.

Hridoy left the field on a stretcher after scoring 42 off 84 deliveries, dealing a blow to Bangladesh's middle order. The partnership added 80 runs off 168 balls.

Litton Das replaced Hridoy at the crease and remained unbeaten on seven alongside Shadman when bad light brought another interruption.

item.title: We move from culture of loan default to culture of looting: Wahiduddin Mahmud
item.description:
Wahiduddin Mahmud, former advisor for planning and education of the interim government, said that the country's banking sector first deteriorated due to the culture of loan defaults.

"Although we had moved away from the culture of non-performing loans, a new ''culture of banking loot'' emerged after 2010. This is why the financial sector is in such a bad state today," Wahiduddin Mahmud made these comments on Wednesday morning, during the inaugural session of the two-day annual banking conference organised by the Bangladesh Institute of Bank Management (BIBM) in Mirpur, Dhaka.

During his speech, Wahiduddin Mahmud shared his experiences on banking sector reforms.

He said, "To move away from the culture of non-performing loans, many rules and regulations were created and reformed with much effort. Alongside, discipline was restored by making rules. We were able to bring some private banks up to international standards. But after that, the culture of banking loot began, which is more severe. Money was taken from banks without any rules."

Wahiduddin Mahmud advised learning from past experiences in the banking sector.

He said, "We need to learn from the many years of experience in the banking sector. Why should we start learning anew? We had many debates in the past. Previously, we allowed banks to be established in the private sector without creating an adequate regulatory framework. What was the consequence of that? We saw that at the time, entrepreneur-directors drew loans of about one-third (equal to 35 per cent) of total deposits from the relevant banks."

Wahiduddin Mahmud stated that there should have been rules about whether a group or family could control multiple banks, which should come under ''anti-trust'' laws. He noted that there is still no antitrust or anti-monopoly law in place.

Influential persons close to political governments have always used state banks as centres for the distribution of undue privileges, according to Wahiduddin Mahmud.

He advised that if a political government wants to distribute benefits for political reasons, they should choose sectors that won't cause large economic damage to the country. However, it is entirely inappropriate to provide political patronage through the banking or financial sector. Political governments must understand this, as there is nothing Bangladesh Bank or bankers can do about it.

Wahiduddin Mahmud mentioned that the hasty approval of new banks after 2010, without proper vetting, led to their bankruptcy.

He explained that some bankrupt banks had accepted deposits from government institutions.

Wahiduddin Mahmud further stated that banks were even opened with teachers' salaries, welfare funds, and pension funds. Eventually, those banks became completely bankrupt, and poor teachers, MPO-listed teachers had billions of their pensions and welfare funds stuck. Those funds are still inaccessible.

Over the past 15 years, the excessive relaxation of regulations in the banking sector has led to the current situation, in Wahiduddin Mahmud's view.

He said, "Now, to rescue weak banks, some relaxation of regulations will again be necessary. But where is the guarantee that by relaxing regulations, we won't end up in the same bad situation as before?"

To overcome the current situation in the banking sector, Wahiduddin Mahmud suggested, "Banks should be given the opportunity to stand on their own feet. However, in doing so, we need to maintain adequate safeguards. Each case should be individually examined to ensure that funds reach honest, genuine entrepreneurs and businesses. If we cannot guarantee this, we will end up falling into the same old pit."

Other speakers are Md Kabir Ahmed, Deputy Governor of Bangladesh Bank; Abdul Hai Sarkar, President of the Bangladesh Association of Banks (BAB) and Chairman of Dhaka Bank; Jean Pesme, Regional Director for Bangladesh and Bhutan at the World Bank; and Masrur Arefin, Chairman of the Association of Bankers, Bangladesh (ABB), and Managing Director (MD) and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of City Bank.

The keynote address was presented by Zaidi Sattar, Chairman of the private research organisation Policy Research Institute (PRI).

item.title: Tarique invites Japanese investment in five key sectors, including rail, technology
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Wednesday invited Japanese companies to invest in five priority sectors in Bangladesh, including automotive manufacturing, energy, technology and space, high-speed rail and logistics, and agro-processing, promising government support and reforms to improve the business environment.
Addressing the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Forum Dialogue at JETRO headquarters in Tokyo, he said the two countries should take their long-standing relationship to a new level through trade and investment after signing the first-ever Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) between Bangladesh and another country.
The forum was jointly organised by the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO) and the Japan-Bangladesh Committee for Commercial and Economic Cooperation (JBCCEC).
Tarique said around 350 Japanese companies are operating in Bangladesh, but Japanese direct investment remained below US$500 million, while Bangladesh’s exports to Japan stood at US$1.36 billion and imports from Japan at US$2.16 billion in the last fiscal year.
Under the recently signed EPA, 7,379 Bangladeshi products will enjoy duty-free access to Japan, while Japanese goods, including steel, automotive parts and electronic components, will receive preferential access to Bangladesh, he said.
The Prime Minister said Bangladesh has a market of more than 180 million people, a young workforce with a median age of 27 and a growing middle class. The country is expected to become one of the world’s top 10 consumer economies by 2030, he added.
He said his government has heard Japanese companies’ concerns over reliable energy, efficient infrastructure, predictable customs clearance and taxation, and was working to address them.
“I fully understand that businesses need certainty. Investors need confidence. Our job is creating the right environment to deliver both,” Tarique said.
On automotive manufacturing, he said Toyota has informed the government earlier this month of its plan to begin work on a vehicle manufacturing facility in Bangladesh, with full production targeted for 2029.
The Prime Minister said the government will provide every possible support for the initiative.
In the energy sector, he invited Japanese companies to invest in LNG infrastructure, efficient gas-fired power generation and renewable energy, saying Bangladesh has short-, medium- and long-term plans for gas and electricity development.
Tarique also highlighted cooperation with Japanese energy company JERA.
He said Bangladesh is planning to establish a Bangladesh-Japan Technology Park focused on innovation in artificial intelligence, cloud computing, robotics and electronics manufacturing, involving Japanese companies, universities and investors.
The Prime Minister also called for cooperation with Japanese institutions in space science, satellite engineering and related technologies to strengthen Bangladesh’s space capabilities.
On rail and logistics, he said Bangladesh plans to develop a nationwide elevated high-speed rail network connecting Dhaka, Chattogram, Sylhet, Rajshahi, Khulna and Barishal.
Tarique said the government plans to prepare a national master plan, assess passenger and freight demand, prioritise routes and conduct feasibility studies, inviting Japanese institutions to invest in the initiative.
He also urged Japanese companies to explore food processing and agro-based manufacturing opportunities in Bangladesh, particularly at the Bangladesh Special Economic Zone in Araihazar, which is being developed by Sumitomo Corporation to Japanese standards.
Emphasising people-to-people ties, the Prime Minister said Bangladesh wants to make Japanese-language education a priority so that millions of young people can learn the language alongside technical skills.
He said skilled Bangladeshi professionals proficient in Japanese can help meet employment needs in both Japan and Bangladesh.
Recalling Japan’s recognition of Bangladesh in February 1972 and its role as the country’s largest development partner for more than five decades, Tarique said the two countries should turn their long-standing friendship into a stronger partnership that creates opportunities for their people and shared prosperity.

item.title: Four killed in Rangpur bus-truck collision, including three garment workers
item.description:
The death toll from a collision between a passenger bus and a parked dump truck in Mithapukur, Rangpur, has risen to four, including three garment workers.
At least 14 others, including women, were injured in the accident and taken to Rangpur Medical College Hospital.
The accident occurred around 5:30am on Wednesday in front of Shah Amanat Petrol Pump at Bairagiganj Bazar in Mithapukur upazila, on the Dhaka-Rangpur highway.
The deceased were identified as Mozaffar Rahman, Golapi Begum and Alamgir Hossain, all from Phulbari upazila in Kurigram, who worked in the garment sector in Dhaka. The fourth victim was identified as Apel, a bus assistant.
According to police and local sources, a Khan Enterprise bus travelling from Dhaka to Bhurungamari in Kurigram rammed into the rear of a soil-laden dump truck parked on the highway.
Police, fire service personnel and local residents took part in rescue operations following the collision. One person died at the scene, while three others succumbed to their injuries after being taken to hospital.
Moazzem Uddin, officer-in-charge of Baradarga Highway Police Station, confirmed the four deaths. He said the seriously injured passengers were receiving medical treatment and traffic on the highway had since returned to normal.
Sardar Abdul Jalil of Rangpur Medical College Hospital also confirmed that three people brought to the hospital after the accident had died.

item.title: PM seeks Japan’s support to diversify Bangladesh’s exports
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Wednesday sought Japan’s cooperation in diversifying Bangladesh’s export basket and expanding trade and investment opportunities as the two countries look to strengthen their economic partnership.
He made the call during a meeting with Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO) President Susumu Kataoka in Tokyo at 11:45am local time, said PM’s Deputy Press Secretary Shahadat Hossain Shadhin.
The Prime Minister also called for increased Japanese investment in Bangladesh’s special economic zones, particularly in advanced manufacturing, ICT, automobiles, renewable energy and agro-processing, as he sought stronger trade and economic ties between the two countries.
He praised JETRO’s role in expanding Japanese investment in Bangladesh, saying new opportunities are emerging for Japanese companies in the country.
Both sides agreed that the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) will play an important role in strengthening bilateral trade and investment ties.
Tarique also called for Japanese support for skills development programmes and the establishment of Japanese language training centres in Bangladesh.
He said such initiatives will help create employment opportunities in Japan and strengthen the long-term economic partnership between the two countries.
JETRO President Susumu Kataoka said Bangladesh has strong investment potential because of its economic growth and geographical location.
He said Japanese companies are already showing interest in doing business and investing in Bangladesh in response to various initiatives taken by the government under Tarique’s leadership.
After the meeting, Tarique attended a luncheon hosted by Kataoka at the latter’s invitation, where they also discussed advancing bilateral cooperation and economic relations.
The Prime Minister invited the JETRO president to visit Bangladesh at his convenience.
The Bangladesh delegation included Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury, Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat, PM’s Adviser on Finance and Planning Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir, State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Aninda Islam Amit, Invest Bangladesh Authority Chairman Ashik Chowdhury, Bangladesh Bank Governor Md Mostaqur Rahman, PM’s Special Assistant Dr Md Shakirul Islam Khan, Additional Press Secretary Atikur Rahman Rumon and other senior officials from the Prime Minister’s Office.

item.title: Gold price rises by Tk2,216 per bhori after four straight cuts
item.description:
The price of gold has gone up again in the domestic market, with the cost of the best-quality 22-carat gold rising by Tk2,216 per bhori.
The new rates came into effect from 10am Wednesday, according to a press release issued by the Bangladesh Jewellers Association (Bajus).
With the latest adjustment, 22-carat gold will now sell at Tk223,074 per bhori including VAT.
Bajus said the prices of gold ornaments were adjusted following an increase in the price of refined (tejabi) gold in the local market.
Under the revised rates, the price of 21-carat gold has been raised by Tk2,100 to Tk213,043 per bhori, while 18-carat gold has gone up by Tk1,750 to Tk182,950 per bhori.
The price of gold of the traditional method has increased by Tk1,458 to Tk149,474 per bhori.
Earlier, Bajus had cut gold prices four times in a row on October 13, 22, 23 and 25, bringing down the price of 22-carat gold by a total of Tk10,439 per bhori. The latest hike comes after those four consecutive reductions.
Meanwhile, silver prices remain unchanged despite the rise in gold rates.
According to the new rates, 22-carat silver will sell at Tk3,849 per bhori, including VAT.
The prices of 21-carat and 18-carat silver stand at Tk3,674 and Tk3,149 per bhori respectively, while silver of the traditional method will cost Tk2,391 per bhori.

item.title: National Summit champions young women’s economic empowerment, leadership in Dhaka
item.description:
Save the Children in Bangladesh, with support from Unicef, hosted the "From Aspiration to Achievement: National Summit on Young Women’s Economic Empowerment and Leadership" on Wednesday in Dhaka.
Held under the Promotion of Women’s Empowerment and Resilience Building (Power) Project, the landmark summit brought together policymakers, government officials, development partners, private sector representatives, civil society organizations, and young women.
The event focused heavily on supporting adolescent girls and young women, particularly those not in education, employment, or training, by strengthening their economic participation, leadership, and resilience.
The day's high-level proceedings also featured remarks from special guest Deepa Sankar, chief of education for Unicef Bangladesh.
Highlighting the critical importance of education and skill development for youth empowerment in Bangladesh, she emphasized that non-formal education and skill training programs should no longer be viewed merely as alternative pathways, but integrated as vital components of the mainstream education system.
Another special guest Kazi Moklesur Rahman, additional secretary of the Ministry of Youth and Sports and project director of the Earn Project, highlighted the scope for institutional synergy.
He expressed his keen interest in integrating the learnings and achievements of Save the Children's Power project into the Ministry’s key initiatives, including the government's Earn project.
Mahdi Amin, adviser to the prime minister, honored the event as chief guest.
He stated that initiatives like Save the Children's Power project inspire the government to further drive the national growth narrative, particularly in youth and women's empowerment.
Emphasizing practical skill application over formal degrees, he noted: "Building practical skills is far more critical than merely acquiring academic certificates. The government is committed to collaborating with development partners like Save the Children to create such practical learning opportunities."
The day-long program featured an inaugural ceremony highlighting inspirational personal journeys shared directly by young women participants, followed by policy dialogues and panel discussions.
Sessions throughout the day centered on strengthening the ecosystem for young women's economic empowerment and bridging the gap between youth and employers for the future of work.
Through collaborative networking, exhibitions, and strategic discussions, the summit sought to chart clear pathways for advancing young women's economic independence and long-term leadership across Bangladesh.

item.title: Dhaka launches clean school pilot in 21 educational institutions
item.description:
The Dhaka district administration has launched a pilot project called “Clean School Teams” at 21 educational institutions to promote cleanliness among students and raise awareness about dengue prevention.
The initiative, which involves five institutions in Dhaka city and others across the district’s 16 upazilas, was inaugurated on Wednesday by Dhaka Divisional Commissioner Md Moniruzzaman Miah in the deputy commissioner’s conference room.
Inspired by Japan’s O-soji model, which encourages people to clean their own surroundings, the initiative aims to instil habits of cleanliness, promote respect for labour and foster a sense of responsibility among students.
Speaking at the inauguration, Moniruzzaman said the model went beyond routine cleaning and could help cultivate discipline and responsibility among students.
“When students develop the habit of keeping their own schools clean, it creates a positive ripple effect in their families and the wider community,” he said.
He added that ensuring a clean and healthy learning environment required the collective participation of teachers, students, parents and other stakeholders.
Addressing concerns about drug abuse and juvenile gangs, the divisional commissioner urged parents and teachers to remain attentive to children’s social circles and encourage them to participate in constructive activities. He said social initiatives should begin in schools and extend to families and the wider community.
Dhaka Deputy Commissioner Farida Khanum said cleanliness was not merely about keeping school premises tidy but also about teaching responsibility, respect for labour and care for the environment.
“A clean school today lays the foundation for conscious and responsible citizens of tomorrow,” she said, adding that small, practical steps could help instil these values in students.
She said the initiative also aligned with the vision of building a “Green and Clean Bangladesh”.
Under the pilot project, participating schools will set aside 15–20 minutes each day for cleaning activities. Students will work in small groups to clean designated areas, including classrooms, corridors and libraries, under teachers’ supervision. School staff will remain responsible for cleaning toilets, drains and other potentially hazardous areas.
The programme will also include weekly inspections to identify dengue risks, such as stagnant water and uncovered containers that could serve as breeding grounds for Aedes mosquitoes. Schools will document their findings and follow-up measures using checklists.
Under the “My Home, My Responsibility” initiative, students will receive weekly checklists encouraging them to keep their living spaces tidy, dispose of waste properly and prevent water from accumulating around their homes. Teachers will review the checklists every Sunday.
Participating schools will introduce waste segregation systems for biodegradable, recyclable and other waste. Students will also learn how to produce organic fertiliser from biodegradable materials.
The administration has proposed a “Clean School Challenge” to assess institutions based on cleanliness, dengue prevention, waste management and student participation. The best-performing schools, classes and students may receive certificates, books, educational materials or saplings.
The project was initiated by Farida Khanum to extend cleanliness practices beyond school premises and encourage students to spread the message among their families and communities.
On July 8, the Dhaka district administration began forming Clean School Teams in educational institutions across the district. A subsequent three-month research period involved reviewing school activities and studying successful cleanliness models in other countries.
The administration then developed an implementation strategy adapted from Japan’s O-soji model to suit Bangladesh’s context.

item.title: Education must remain inclusive
item.description:
We agree with Education and Primary and Mass Education Minister Dr ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon that religious education can play a significant role in shaping more responsible citizens.
Integrating moral values, integrity, and spiritual literacy into national curricula can certainly help stem social degradation and foster conscientious youth. Merely striving for efficiency and growth are meaningless if fellow citizens lack empathy and care.
With that said, in a nation built upon pluralism and constitutional guarantees of equal rights, regardless of one’s religion or faith, state policy regarding moral and religious education must strictly reflect our diverse national fabric.
If we are to educate our children about religion and faith, and expect them to be able to take the lessons they provide, then we must simultaneously ensure that no single faith receives majoritarian preference while neglecting the rest.
Bangladesh is home to millions of Hindu, Buddhist, Christian, and ethnic minority citizens, among other faiths, whose traditions and values are integral to our national identity.
As such, when state officials frame moral development through the prism of a single religion, they risk alienating minority students and eroding the inclusive foundation of public education.
Every child attending a state school or general institution deserves access to moral instruction that honours, reflects, and respects their own heritage and faith, rather than being subjected to a standardized framework that treats non-majority traditions as an afterthought.
Modernizing our national education system therefore requires a delicate balance between core ethical values and secular inclusivity.
While streamlining madrasa education with mainstream science, arts, and technology is a welcome effort to bridge structural disparities that have existed for too long, national policy must also ensure that general public schools remain welcoming spaces for students of all backgrounds.
A truly progressive curriculum must emphasize universal values -- integrity, tolerance, civic responsibility, and mutual respect -- alongside comprehensive, high-quality instruction regarding students’ respective faiths. That should be the goal.

item.title: Parties must prioritize national stability
item.description:
The attack on the central office of the Communist Party of Bangladesh (CPB) in Dhaka’s Paltan area is a deeply disturbing reminder of the partisan hostility still poisoning our political landscape.
When political offices are stormed, vandalized, or targeted by mobs over alleged slogans or ideological grievances, democratic norms are fundamentally violated.
Reverting to street-level violence, intimidation, and reflexive mudslinging exposes a reckless disregard for civil order at a time when the nation can least afford political instability.
Instead of taking immediate responsibility or condemning mob behaviour, the immediate aftermath of the incident reduced to predictable finger-pointing, partisan denial, and blame-shifting.
This toxic reflex must end if we are to make any progress as a nation.
Political parties across the spectrum - whether in government or opposition - must recognize that their primary duty is to the citizens of Bangladesh, not to settle petty political scores or establish dominance through intimidation.
At a moment when the country is confronting severe economic pressures, turning political rivalries into physical clashes is an unpardonable distraction from the urgent work of national governance.
Allowing partisan mobs to operate with impunity under the guise of political grievance invites lawlessness and further fractures. Violence cannot be normalized as a tool for political expression.
Law enforcement agencies must investigate the Paltan attack with absolute impartiality, identifying and prosecuting the perpetrators regardless of their political affiliations.
The leadership of all political parties must also issue an unequivocal, zero-tolerance directive to their cadres against mob violence and political thuggery.
Bangladesh's democratic space has all but eroded, and we cannot think of reviving it if political dissent is met with bricks and iron rods. It is time for our political parties to focus their energies on what matters -- constructive policy, economic stabilization, and public service.

item.title: Spain: At least 10 dead in high-speed train crash
item.description:
At least 10 people were killed in a train crash in central Spain on Wednesday morning, local authorities have confirmed.
“The information we are receiving is not good at all,” a spokeswoman for the government of the Castilla-La Mancha region told local media. “There are at least 10 dead and it is possible that the number will increase.”
“There has been a collision between two trains [and] there are injured people,” added Manuel Galans, mayor of the town of Urda in the province of Toledo, near to where the incident took place just after 9am local time.
The mayor of another nearby village, Jesus Perez of Los Yebenes, told Spanish TV that the accident appeared “serious.”
Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia told local broadcaster TVE that it was a “high impact accident, it will be a major tragedy” but said it was too soon to confirm a final casualty figure.
“We don’t just need help from nearby hospitals, we need nearby hospitals that have ICU beds,” she added.
The cause of the collision was not immediately known, but initial reports suggested one train had slammed into the back of another train which had been stationary.
Images from the scene showed at least two severely damaged train carriages flipped over on their side after tumbling down an embankment.
One of the trains, operated by AVE, was reportedly carrying 397 passengers while the other, operated by IRYO, had 146 people on board, according to the Castilla-La Mancha local government spokeswoman.
A reporter for local broadcaster TVE described scenes of “absolute chaos” and a constant stream of ambulances and emergency vehicles.
El Pais cited witnesses describing numerous injuries and ​arrival of emergency medical teams at the scene.
“All resources are currently being deployed,” spokesperson for the Spanish emergency services told the AFP news agency, including “several fire crews, three helicopters, and two mobile intensive care units.”
In a post on social media, rail operator Adif confirmed that “traffic ​on the Madrid-Andalusia high-speed rail line ​has been suspended following a rear-end collision ​between two trains.”
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said he was “shocked” by the “serious” accident.
“Emergency services are working on the ground to assist those affected and ensure their safety, in coordination with all the involved administrations,” he wrote on social media. “My affection, solidarity and support to all the victims and their families.”
It’s not the first train crash in Spain this year. In January, 45 people died when a train jumped the track and hit an oncoming train.

item.title: Three killed by storm in southern India
item.description:
Ferocious winds and torrential rain lashed India’s southeastern coast after a cyclone made landfall on Wednesday, killing at least three people before the storm weakened, officials said.
Cyclone Arnab hit southeastern Andhra Pradesh state as a “very severe cyclonic storm,” with winds of 125-135 kilometers (77-84 miles) per hour and gusts reaching 150 kph in the early hours of Wednesday morning, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said.
Torrential rain was recorded -- as much as 30 centimeters (nearly 12 inches) in parts of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha states, IMD said, with the storm weakening into a “deep depression” throughout Wednesday afternoon.
“Three people have lost their lives, and 31 homes have been damaged,” Narendra Singh Bundela, Inspector General of India’s National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) told reporters.
Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister Nara Chandrababu Naidu thanked officials who had “worked tirelessly throughout the night.”
Around 50,000 people were told to move to safer areas in Andhra Pradesh and another 48,000 in neighboring Odisha.
“Our homes get flooded, and we have to stay in the water,” said Rajeshwari, 65, who gave only one name and had been taken to a government-run shelter near Kakinada.
Overnight, gales battered trees and heavy rain lashed the port city of Kakinada, close to the heart of the storm, as powerful waves crashed ashore.
Residents on Wednesday emerged onto flooded streets to what appeared to be limited damage in the city.
Emergency officials were also busy clearing uprooted trees and other debris from affected roads in the coastal region.
“Thank God, there was not as much damage this time,” said businessman Hussain, 43, who uses one name.
Sadiq, 40, a Kakinanda city resident, told AFP that the situation had become “very dangerous” on Tuesday night, but early warnings from authorities had helped people prepare.
“Many people locked their houses and moved to safer places”, he said.
Cyclones, called hurricanes in the North Atlantic and typhoons in the Pacific, are a regular menace in the Bay of Bengal and northern Indian Ocean.
The storm season, however, has been turbocharged by the El Nino weather phenomenon that has contributed to unprecedented warming.
Neighbouring Sri Lanka and Nepal had also issued warnings.
Nepal’s disaster authority warned that the storm would move inland towards the Himalayas, bringing heavy rainfall and “a high risk of heavy snowfall, snowstorms and avalanches”.
Nepal is still recovering from a catastrophic August 26 flood triggered by a glacial mountain collapse, which killed more than 1,400 people and left over 5,000 missing.

item.title: Trump says Putin-Zelensky meeting to be set up ‘very soon’
item.description:
US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky would be set up “very soon.”
The announcement came as Trump’s administration ramps up diplomatic efforts aimed at ending the Russia-Ukraine war, now in its fifth year.
“There’ll be a meeting set up very soon and I think a lot of progress could be made,” Trump told reporters.
Zelensky said on Sunday that a trilateral meeting between Kyiv, Washington and Moscow would take place in November, aiming to restart stalled peace talks.
The Kremlin had previously said that a meeting between the three countries was planned to take place in the United Arab Emirates in November.
Putin, who ordered the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, has consistently rejected face-to-face talks with Zelensky and insisted Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.
Trump came to power in January 2025 promising to end the war in 24 hours -- but over a year of US-led talks have failed to produce a breakthrough, with tens of thousands killed.
In recent days Trump has once again pivoted away from Ukraine and back to Putin, trumpeting what he said was a deal for Russia to sell diesel and reduce prices sent soaring by his Iran war.

item.title: Netanyahu bloc leads as Israeli votes counted, but no majority
item.description:
The camp of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was ahead of his rival's opposition bloc but still short of a majority on Wednesday after two-thirds of the votes were counted in Israel's pivotal general election.
Voters turned out in the highest numbers in decades to give their verdict on Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, who has pushed the country sharply to the right and unleashed a wave of wars in response to Hamas's October 7, 2023 resistance campaign.
Following the vote, both Netanyahu and his main rival Gadi Eisenkot vowed to form a government despite neither being projected to win a majority.
With 66% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's bloc was shown to have 54 of the 120 seats in the parliament.
Eisenkot's opposition bloc had 48 seats and the country's non-aligned Arab parties 18. The partial results are likely to change as more votes are counted.
Exit polls had shown that Eisenkot, a former military chief and political novice, and his opposition bloc were neck-and-neck with Netanyahu's hard-right camp, with both winning about 51 seats, well away from the threshold for a majority.
The strongest gains went to Arab Israeli parties whose voters turned out in soaring numbers against Netanyahu, who has relentlessly warned that the minority would dilute the Jewish nationalist direction in which he has taken Israel.
The partial results suggest that Eisenkot's bloc would have enough seats for a majority if it entered into a coalition agreement with the Arab parties, something most of its members expressed reluctance to do on the campaign trail.
But Yair Golan, the head of Israel's main left-wing party, which is part of Eisenkot's camp, called for precisely that on Wednesday.
"We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said on X. "We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens."
Eisenkot had said during the campaign he would not govern with Israeli Arab lawmakers, echoing the position of Netanyahu, who has suggested a government relying on Arab votes would lack legitimacy.
Arab lawmakers could also give Eisenkot support in parliamentary votes on an ad hoc basis, enabling him to maintain a minority government without joining a coalition.
A lack of clear majority for either camp could mean weeks spent trying to cobble together coalitions, with possible new elections on the horizon if negotiations fail.
A stalemate could in the immediate term benefit Netanyahu, who would remain caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed.
Full results are expected by Thursday evening or Friday morning.
Netanyahu, greeting cheering supporters at a Jerusalem convention centre after 3am (0100 GMT) on Wednesday morning, called for a "strong government of the right" and said the "Jewish and Zionist majority must unite."
The 77-year-old prime minister, who has governed Israel on and off for nearly two decades, was unusually brief and did not directly claim victory.
US President Donald Trump claimed on Wednesday that his endorsement of Netanyahu had helped "a lot."
Speaking to supporters in Tel Aviv, 66-year-old Eisenkot issued a warning to Netanyahu, who observers say could use renewed war to push for a unity government.
"Netanyahu, don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.
He called Netanyahu "a caretaker prime minister, without a mandate or the people's trust."
The vote came as Israel faces increasing isolation on the world stage, driven by the wars in Iran and Gaza, as well as soaring settlement construction and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
Eisenkot shares many of Netanyahu's views on security and has backed the Gaza offensive that has reduced the territory to rubble.
But he has vowed to create a more inclusive atmosphere inside Israel, repair its international standing and rein in violent West Bank settlers.
After a turnout of nearly 78 percent, the highest since 1999, Eisenkot said it would be a mistake to hold a second election and vowed to work "swiftly" to form a government.
"The public has voted for change," he said. "A worthy leader would accept the people's vote of no confidence and announce his retirement from political life today."
Exit polls had shown Israeli Arab lists projected to win 18 or 19 seats, a sharp gain.
Arab Israelis, also known as Palestinian citizens of Israel, account for about 21% of the country's population.
